[0] everyday_reading (E): In maths classes a transition matrix is often written column-wise (column = from), and "matrix" suggests a table of counts; in SW p[i][j] is a probability, row i = the page the surfer is on, column j = the page moved to, and each row sums to 1.
[1] misconception (M) -> MultidimensionalArray: wrong rule: A 2-D array is one thing, not an array of arrays. Right rule: Java represents p[][] as an array of N row arrays; p[page] is itself a 1-D double array (the distribution used by the random move).
[2] misconception (M) -> NoJaggedArrays: wrong rule: Multi-dimensional arrays must be rectangular. Right rule: Each row is its own array, so rows can differ in length (a ragged array); the transition matrix is created square with new double[N][N].
[3] misconception (M) -> RowsNeedNotSumToOne: wrong rule: A page with no outgoing links can have an all-zero row. Right rule: Every row must be a probability distribution summing to 1; a page with no links gets 1/N in every column.

[0] names_the_element (N): A data structure: an N-by-N two-dimensional double array p[][] (a stochastic matrix) whose entry p[i][j] is the probability of moving from page i to page j.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Entry (i, j) is the probability that the surfer on page i moves to page j; by the 90-10 rule it is .90*counts[i][j]/outDegree[i] + .10/N, and every row is a discrete probability distribution summing to 1.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Three steps in order: read N and create counts[][] and outDegree[]; read all links and accumulate counts; then, row by row (outer i) and column by column (inner j), compute and print one probability; the header "N N" is printed before the rows.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Output is a matrix file: the row and column counts, then N rows of N doubles printed with %8.5f; for tiny.txt row 0 is 0.02000 0.92000 0.02000 0.02000 0.02000 and row 1 is 0.02000 0.02000 0.38000 0.38000 0.20000.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One inner-loop pass evaluates one double p for the current (i, j) from counts[i][j], outDegree[i] and N, and prints it; no array is modified by this phase.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Row i depends only on the tallies read for page i (counts[i][] and outDegree[i]); the matrix cannot be computed until all links have been read.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Dividing counts[i][j] by outDegree[i] (after scaling by .90) and adding .10/N is the normalisation that makes row i sum to 1; the double operand .90 keeps the division from being integer division.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): The random move reads one row p[page] as a 1-D array and accumulates its entries; it only works if that row sums to 1.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): The matrix is double[N][N]: p[i] is the row array for page i and p[i][j] an element; indices must be in 0..N-1 and the first index is the row (from-page).
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): A matrix whose rows are probability distributions defines a Markov chain: the next page depends only on the current page's row.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): Transition's formula is valid only if every outDegree[i] > 0; a page with no outlinks must have its row filled with 1/N.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): The .10/N term, added to every entry, is the teleport (random-page) part of each row; the .90 factor scales the link part so the two parts sum to 1.
[7] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Specifies completely the surfer's behaviour as data; Transition is a filter turning the list-of-links representation into a matrix that RandomSurfer and Markov both read.

[0] predict_a_change (C): Invariant: every row sums to 1. Changing the split to 80-20 or 95-5 keeps it (the two weights still sum to 1) but changes the ranks; changing .10/N to .10, or omitting the leap term, breaks it.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Right tool when the model has few enough pages that N*N doubles fit in memory and both simulation and the power method need per-pair probabilities; not for millions of pages (trillions of entries).
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: outDegree[i] must be > 0 (no dangling pages). Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A page with no outlinks: .90*counts[i][j] is the double 0.0 and 0.0/0 gives NaN, so the whole row prints NaN with no exception.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Each row must sum to 1. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Any row whose entries do not sum to 1 (wrong scaling, missing leap term, unhandled dangling page) makes the RandomSurfer move fail.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Indices i, j must be in 0..N-1. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Link with page >= N, or loop bound <= N: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

The links read from input fill counts[i][j], and each row of the transition matrix is built from those counts.
The 90-10 rule says the surfer follows a random link 90 percent of the time and jumps to a random page 10 percent of the time, and each transition-matrix entry is computed from it.
Transition assumes that every page has an outgoing link; Exercise 1.6.3 handles a page with no outgoing links by filling its row of the transition matrix with 1/N.
The transition matrix specifies the probability of each move, and the random process those probabilities define is a Markov chain.
Each row of the transition matrix must be a probability distribution, so counts[i][j] is divided by outDegree[i] (scaled by .90, plus .10/N) to make row i sum to 1.
Row p[i] is the probability distribution used to choose the next page when the surfer is on page i.
The transition matrix is a 2-D double array p[i][j], with one row array per page.
